newsitem.title: UK: Pragmatic UK markets look for Labour by-election win.
newsitem.headline: Pragmatic UK markets look for Labour by-election win.

text.p: In the richest of ironies, British financial markets could be hoping for a landslide victory for the opposition Labour Party in a key by-election this week.

The constituency of Wirral South is up for grabs on Thursday and is widely expected to be won by the opposition Labour Party, pushing the Conservative government into a minority in parliament in the process.
Traditionally, that would be a cue for Britain's markets to sell off, spooked by fears of a high spending, tax raising Labour government.
Times have changed and so has the Labour Party and the markets have discounted a Labour victory at this by-election and probably the general election, which must be held by May.
But the main reason why Britain's markets may respond well to a Labour win on the Wirral is that only thing they hate more than a left wing government is uncertainty.

"Wirral South is a foregone conclusion," said Kevin Adams, gilts analyst at BZW. "But it could be market-positive in that a really convincing victory for Labour in what is really a true-blue Tory stronghold will allay fears of a hung parliament. If the Conservatives win, everything will be up in the air."
Nothing would create more uncertainty than a general election which fails to produce a majority for any one party -- leaving a hung parliament.
And with Prime Minister John Major's beleaguered government trailing by up to 20 points in the opinion polls, a hung parliament is probably the best it can hope for.

"The worst scenario for the market is the one in the middle," said Rob Buckland, UK equity strategist at HSBC James Capel. "The market can live with a Labour majority that everyone is expecting, it would probably prefer a Conservative majority, but it doesn't want something in between."

The Wirral seat, in a prosperous corner of northwest England, was a safe one for the government. Conservative MP Barry Porter held a majority of more than 8,000 but died late last year, forcing this week's vote.
Ideally, of course, most of those who work in the markets would love to see Major swept back into power for another five years. But that looks unlikely.

The Conservative Party has always been the darling of the markets. In its 18 years of unbroken rule, it has presided over the deregulation of Britain's financial markets and the explosion of activity that resulted. London is now unchallenged as Europe's major financial centre.
It has widened share ownership to millions of people and helped the golden boys of the City pull in huge salaries and sometimes even bigger bonuses.

At the last election in 1992, opinion polls pointed to a Labour victory but Prime Minister John Major snatched victory from the jaws of defeat. In London's square mile, the financial heart of the city, champagne flowed for days.
The polls got it wrong last time, but this time Labour is streets ahead, not just a handful of percentage points, a fact the markets have taken on board.
Of course, the Labour Party is a very different political animal nowadays and much less of a worry for the markets.
Gone are the days of tax and spend. Now, shadow Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown promises no income tax rises and pledges to stick to Tory spending plans for the next two years.

In some areas, Labour even outdo the Tories. "The markets view a Labour victory positively, a remarkable achievement by (Labour leader Tony) Blair and Brown" said Dick Howard, senior economist at fund managers Julius Baer Investments.
"Policies such as a more positive attitude towards the single European currency, greater Bank of England independence and tight public spending targets are all gilt-friendly."

And Brown can probably get away without pushing interest rates too much higher either. The pound's stellar rally -- up about 16 percent in little more than six months -- is keeping inflation under wraps by depressing import prices.

But doubts remain about Labour's ability to keep a tight control of the public purse strings. They are bound to come under pressure from their old allies, the trade unions, after years of public sector pay restraints.
Howard thinks gilt prices will peak around election night. "Gilt investors should ride the rollercoaster for now but prepare to exit before Labour's May Day celebrations."
